messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
At twelve, Elena had learned to read her childhood home by its sounds and its scents. The domestic violence she witnessed was not merely loud; it was thick with the heavy, sour smell of her father’s sweat as he paced the hallway, and her mother’s quiet, trembling body when the fighting finally settled. Elena remembered the event in sharp, unblinking pictures: the glint of a shattered glass tumbler on the linoleum, the dark spill of her mother’s hair over her knees, the sudden lunge of an arm that made the light fixture swing. What frightened her most was the sheer unpredictability of the shouting, which could erupt at any hour, and the sudden, heavy touch when her family would grab her wrist to pull her clear, their skin warm and damp against hers. She had come to believe that the noise and the scent were not just background details, but persistent signals that something was about to break. Those childhood cues remain steady in her perception, woven into her daily work as a detective. When she steps into the precinct, the ambient sweat of her colleagues on the morning shift hits her like a physical pressure. She backs toward the perimeter walls, always choosing seats that face the door and leave her flank protected against the main thoroughfare. Unexpected movement across the room—a uniformed officer stepping out of an elevator, another detective turning from a file cabinet—sends a jolt through her shoulders. She wakes during the night, eyes sharp in the dark, checking the bedroom door and the space beneath the bed to verify that she is safe. Her partner, Mateo, has learned to approach her from the side, yet even his casual brush of fingers against her forearm makes her freeze. She grows weary of any feeling, whether the sharp pang of grief or the quiet warmth of Mateo’s affection, and often retreats into a careful numbness, refusing to engage until the emotional temperature of a room matches her own. She presses a thumbnail into the pad of her index finger when the pictures crowd her mind, the sharp sting pulling her attention away from the event, and she sidesteps any contact that feels uninvited. When Elena tries to remember what happened, the memories resist her deliberate effort. When asked to describe the event in a clinical setting, she touches her temple and says, “It doesn’t come as a story. It just drops into my head.” The event surfaces as disconnected pictures that demand immediate attention, and she finds it difficult to access them when she tries to pull them forward on purpose. The sight of a man’s damp collar or a raised voice at a traffic light pulls her under, and when the pictures finally surface, an overwhelming grief washes through her. She had come to believe that her constant reactions mean she is going crazy, that her mind is unraveling rather than adapting. She questions her own judgment in familiar situations, second-guessing whether her caution is warranted, and she holds a quiet conviction that the event happened to her because of the sort of person she is. The images are sharp and specific, while the deliberate attempt to grasp them feels like trying to hold water. Her work keeps her in environments that echo her past. On patrol and in interview rooms, the physical demands of the job force contact she actively avoids. Over the past several months, this avoidance has marked out a quiet distance in her personal life. She begins declining family dinners where laughter grows loud and hands reach across the table, and she takes long lunch shifts to eat alone in her car, parked facing the exit. The precinct’s physical therapy room, with its mirrored walls and frequent brushing of arms between colleagues, becomes a place she navigates with deliberate, guarded steps. The space around her has narrowed, but the functions of her days continue without collapse. It is the accumulation of these steady, unyielding moments that has finally brought Elena to the clinic. She is tired of explaining her flinches, of watching her colleagues’ eyes drop to her self-inflicted marks when she thinks no one is looking. What she wants most is not to erase the pictures or silence the alarms, but to understand why they keep pulling her attention. She fears that without help, she will remain trapped in a state of perpetual readiness, forever checking the door, forever guarding her skin, forever certain that the shouting and the scent are closer than they really are.
